title: Cast thy bread (Ecclesiastes 11:1)
hook: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days"
carry: thou knowest not which shall prosper

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet said eat thy bread with joy, and do it with thy might. Today the same book sends the bread down a river.

Bread, tossed from a riverbank onto moving water. It floats a second, turns, and the current takes it. By any normal reckoning, that bread is gone. Nobody gets a receipt from a river. Yet near the end of Ecclesiastes, the book that kept saying all is breath, comes this odd instruction: "Cast thy bread upon the waters, For thou shalt find it after many days." Let it go, says the teacher, and it will come back to you.
screen: `BREAD ON MOVING WATER.` → `NO RECEIPT FROM A RIVER.` → `IT WILL COME BACK.`

segments.voice: The verse never says how the bread comes back, or when, beyond after many days. So readers fill the gap in different ways. Some hear a merchant's advice: send your goods across the sea, and the profit returns in time. Some hear charity: give to people who can never repay you, and the good finds its way home. The commentator Rashi reads it as kindness done for someone you expect never to see again. The next verse keeps the hand open: "Divide a portion into seven, yea, even into eight; For thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth." Not one gift, carefully placed. Seven shares, and then one more. Then Kohelet turns to the person who waits for perfect conditions: "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; And he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap." Stand in the field checking the sky, and the seed stays in the bag. Then the line that ties it together: "In the morning sow thy seed, And in the evening withhold not thy hand; For thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that." Notice what the teacher doesn't promise. He doesn't say every gift returns. He says you don't know. That not-knowing, which earlier in the book made everything feel like breath, becomes here the reason to keep giving. The bread on the water isn't an investment with a guaranteed return. It's a gift, let go.
screen: `HOW IT COMES BACK IS NEVER SAID.` · `SEVEN, YEA, EVEN EIGHT.` · then, large: `WHO WATCHES THE WIND WON'T SOW.` · then: `YOU DON'T KNOW, SO KEEP GIVING.`

segments.voice: Let one small gift come to mind that you could give with no way to know where it lands: a kind word to a stranger, a donation no one will thank you for, an honest compliment to someone you may never see again. Hold it lightly, the way you'd hold bread before you toss it, and decide not to stand on the bank watching the water afterward. If you pray, you can send the gift off with a word of prayer.
Sow. Ecclesiastes' advice to give and let go, casting your bread and sowing your seed before you know what will grow. Today's word.
Your line: thou knowest not which shall prosper. Bread on the water is a gift, not a loan. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Jewish commentators read Ecclesiastes 11:1 as a teaching about kindness and tzedakah given with no promise of return; in some communities the book of Ecclesiastes is read aloud in synagogue on Sukkot.

fork.setup: you've got bread in your hand and a river in front of you. Kohelet is watching. what does he tell you?
options: keep it. bread in the hand is safer.
wait until the current looks right.

what it means: give and let go; Ecclesiastes says you'll find it after many days.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew verb is send, and some readers hear a merchant's cargo, others a kindness to a stranger.

chat.says: What does 'cast thy bread upon the waters' actually mean?
options: Give generously and let it go, since Kohelet says you can't know which gift will prosper.
Get rid of what you don't need; the bread on the water is just waste to toss out.
Wait to give until conditions look right, the way a careful farmer watches the clouds.
